replacement: “Gentlemen,” he said, loudly, almost shouting, yet stumbling over every word, “I ... I’m all right! Don’t be afraid!” he exclaimed. “I—nothing’s the matter,” he said, suddenly turning to Grushenka, who had shrunk back in her chair toward Kalganov and was gripping his hand. “I ... I’m coming, too. I’m here till morning. Gentlemen, may I stay with you till morning? Only till morning, one last time, in this very room?”

“Heavens! I thought he was going to start in again!” Grushenka said nervously. “Listen, Mitya,” she went on, pressing him, “stop prancing about. But it’s nice that you’ve brought champagne. I’d like some myself, and I can’t bear liqueurs. And best of all, you’re here yourself. We were dreadfully bored.... You’ve come on a spree again, I suppose? But put that money away. Where did you get so much?”

The Pole on the sofa impressed him with his dignified manner and his Polish accent, and most of all with his pipe. “Well, so what? It’s a good thing he smokes a pipe,” he thought. The Pole’s puffy, middle-aged face, with its tiny nose and its two very thin, pointed, dyed, cheeky-looking mustaches, hadn’t raised the slightest suspicion in Mitya so far. He wasn’t even particularly struck by the man’s ridiculous wig, made in Siberia, with love-locks combed foolishly forward over the temples. “It must be all right, since he wears a wig,” he went on, musing blissfully. The other Pole, the younger one, was staring at the company with insolent defiance and listening to the talk in silent contempt. He impressed Mitya only by his great height, which made a striking contrast with the Pole on the sofa. “If he stood up, he’d be six foot three.” The thought flitted through Mitya’s head. It also occurred to him that this man must be the other’s friend, a kind of “bodyguard,” and that the big Pole was no doubt at the service of the little Pole with the pipe. But all this seemed to Mitya perfectly proper and not to be questioned. In his doglike mood of submission, every feeling of rivalry had died out.
